sections.heading: C — Defensive driving and weather
sections.markdown:
## C — Defensive driving and weather (part one)

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A01
Be especially alert for stopped vehicles on an interstate, and if your own vehicle becomes disabled move as far off the road as possible, turn on the four-way flashers to show that you are stopped, and get everyone out of the vehicle and well away from the road [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A01
Place one flare about one vehicle length behind a disabled vehicle and another about three hundred feet back, each on the shoulder near the edge of the through lane [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A01
Fog in patches or as a haze reduces visibility, and when the fog is very dense it may be better to leave the interstate and finish the trip on slower roads [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A01
After a crash in heavy fog get your vehicle as far off the road as possible, because leaving it on the road until the police arrive invites further crashes [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A01
Never make a U-turn on an interstate but go to the next exit to turn around, because the gravel or paved crossovers in highway medians are only for police and emergency vehicles [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A01
Construction and maintenance zones on interstates and expressways frequently close one or more lanes and slow or stop traffic, so obey the special speed limits, traffic control signs and flaggers, and when lane-closure signs appear well in advance move to the open lane as soon as possible rather than at the last minute [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A01
In a construction zone the route is often different, the road rougher, and large equipment and busy workers are close to your vehicle, so those workers count on you to drive cautiously and courteously and to follow the signs and flaggers that set the right speed for the conditions [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A02
Defensive driving means being prepared through the practice of good driving habits, which are as easy to form as bad ones and should begin the moment you step into the vehicle and be used on every trip, short or long [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A02
Bad driving habits come from laziness, impatience, inattention, arrogance and aggressiveness, and a driver who shows any of them must evaluate and adjust that behavior to drive safely [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A02
A lazy driver looks only in the rear view mirror instead of turning the head to look behind before changing lanes, pulling away from the curb or getting out on the traffic side, and failing to signal before turning, changing lanes or leaving the curb is a related bad habit that can cause a serious crash [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A02
Regardless of traffic you must come to a complete stop at a stop sign or red light even when turning right, and an impatient driver who speeds from stop to stop, weaves through traffic and tailgates disrupts traffic and raises the chance of a crash without realizing it [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A02
A good driver sits up straight with a firm grip on the wheel, knows where the vehicle is and watches developing traffic problems, because a driver who leans back, loosens the grip and lets attention wander lets the vehicle wander too, and driving with an arm out the window, chatting, gesturing or ignoring the traffic flow marks an inattentive driver [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A03
While the impatient driver is simply in a hurry, the arrogant or aggressive driver is purposely in a hurry, treats the vehicle as an extension of the ego, shows little respect for traffic laws or the rights of others, and should neither be imitated nor competed with [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A03
Concentration is one of the most important elements of safe driving, so the driver's seat is no place for daydreaming, mental napping, window shopping, scenic viewing or distracting conversation, because driving an automobile is a full-time job [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A03
Too much natural light, such as driving east at sunrise or west at sunset, calls for the sun visor, sunglasses, reduced speed and extra alertness, and sunglasses also help on bright summer or winter days against glare from other vehicles' glass and chrome or from snow [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A03
At night and on overcast or rainy days turn on your headlights, not just your parking lights, as soon as it begins to get dark or whenever fog, smoke or extreme cloudiness impairs visibility, because lighting up a little early helps other drivers see you, and keep the lighting system clean and in repair [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A03
Over driving your headlights means driving too fast to stop safely within the distance your headlights clearly light [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A03
Looking directly into oncoming headlights causes momentary blindness, so when meeting a vehicle at night slow down, keep to the right of your lane and look well ahead at the right edge of the road, dimming your beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet of a vehicle you are following [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0072]

sections.heading: C — Defensive driving and weather
sections.markdown:
## C — Defensive driving and weather (part two)

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A04
Turning on your headlights during rain or reduced visibility is required by law and increases your visibility to others [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A04
Wet pavement is most dangerous at the start of a light rain, when oil, dirt and water form a slippery film that weakens road contact on curves and lengthens stopping distance, so reduce your speed [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A04
On wet pavement tires wipe the road like a windshield wiper at speeds up to thirty-five miles per hour, a standard passenger vehicle begins to hydroplane partially at about thirty-five miles per hour, and at fifty-five miles per hour the tires ride entirely on the water film, leaving no friction to brake, accelerate or corner [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A04
In a severe rainstorm tires lose all contact with the road at fifty-five miles per hour, and a gust of wind, a curve or a slight turn can then create an uncontrollable skid [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A04
To reduce hydroplaning slow down in rainstorms, on slushy roads and in standing water, keep tires properly inflated and replace them when the tread wear indicators show, because deep treads let water escape and can prevent complete hydroplaning at normal highway speeds [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A04
Never drive across a flooded roadway, because as little as six inches of water can float some smaller vehicles and two feet of water will carry most vehicles away, after which the vehicle may roll and fill with water, trapping everyone inside [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F25 | anchor: A04
Motorists trapped in their vehicles account for nearly half of all flash flood deaths in the United States, victims often drive straight off the edge of an eroded road without knowing it is gone, and flooding is especially hard to recognize at night [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F26 | anchor: A04
If your vehicle stalls on a flooded roadway leave it immediately and seek higher ground, because it is better to be wet than dead [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F27 | anchor: A04
Keep snow tires or chains ready in winter but remember that neither allows safe driving on snow or ice at normal speeds, so slow down and keep a safe distance, since stopping on snow or ice can take up to twelve times the normal distance and bridges and overpasses may be icy when all other pavement is clear [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F28 | anchor: A04
Keep every window clear of ice and snow, keep the windshield wipers and defroster in good working order, and never start driving until all windows are clear and completely defrosted [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F29 | anchor: A05
When stopping or slowing on ice or packed snow apply the brakes gently and smoothly, a vehicle with anti-lock brakes keeps its steering while braking, but in a vehicle without them you cannot steer unless you pump the brakes by applying and releasing them several times, and you release the brakes at the first hint that the wheels are slipping [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F30 | anchor: A05
When starting on snow or ice keep engine speed low, accelerate slowly and smoothly, let out a manual clutch slowly and shift smoothly, and once moving test the brakes at low speed to learn how slippery the road is and adjust your speed to it [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F31 | anchor: A05
Strong winds can down power lines and trees and blow debris into your path, and crosswinds can be strong enough to force your vehicle into the oncoming lane or off the roadway [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F32 | anchor: A05
Fog is extremely hazardous and smoke from factories, forest fires or burning leaves acts the same way, so in fog or dense smoke reduce speed, be ready for an emergency stop, use low-beam headlights and the wipers, and if your vision is impaired pull off the road, stop, leave the lights on and turn on the hazard lights [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F33 | anchor: A05
Road conditions to consider are mainly matters of construction such as curves, hills, pavement width, multiple lanes, road surfaces, poorly marked or unmarked roads, shoulders and drop-offs [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F34 | anchor: A05
You cannot safely drive ten feet or ten miles in an unsafe vehicle, so West Virginia requires every vehicle to be inspected every two years at a station displaying the official state inspection sign, and the windshield sticker showing the month and year of the next inspection must never be removed [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0074]

items.why: Breakdown steps, light rules, hydroplaning speeds, flood depths and winter braking techniques are recall items served by standard flashcards and quiz questions, so no separate practice mode is needed.

corpus_stability.reason: The West Virginia Driver's Licensing Handbook is a periodically revised official edition, so its defensive-driving and weather pages change at most with a new edition.
